abstract: Language model (LM) agents are increasingly being used to automate complicated tasks in digital environments. Just as humans benefit from powerful software applications, such as integrated development environments, for complex tasks like software engineering, we posit that LM agents represent a new category of end users with their own needs and abilities, and would benefit from specially-built interfaces to the software they use. We investigate how interface design affects the performance of language model agents. As a result of this exploration, we introduce SWE-agent: a system that facilitates LM agents to autonomously use computers to solve software engineering tasks. SWE-agent’s custom agent-computer interface (ACI) significantly enhances an agent’s ability to create and edit code files, navigate entire repositories, and execute tests and other programs. We evaluate SWE-agent on SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both with a pass@$1$ rate of $12.5$% and $87.7$%, respectively, far exceeding the previous state-of-the-art achieved with non-interactive LMs. Finally, we provide insight on how the design of the ACI can impact agents’ behavior and performance.

sections.body: The paper argues that language model agents need interfaces built for them, not only the shell that people use. In the Linux shell setting, agents struggled to edit small file segments and received no feedback on invalid edits. The authors introduce SWE-agent, an agent plus an agent-computer interface (ACI) with a small set of commands for viewing, searching and editing files, along with guardrails and concise feedback. With GPT-4 Turbo, SWE-agent resolves 12.47% of SWE-bench test tasks, against a previous best of 3.8% for a non-interactive retrieval-augmented system. On an ablation subset, SWE-agent solves 10.7 percentage points more instances than the baseline agent that uses only the default Linux shell.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Language model agents struggle with raw Linux shell actions, so the paper proposes a tailored agent-computer interface for software engineering.

sections.body: The section argues that language model agents are a separate class of end user, so interfaces designed for humans may not suit them. An agent-computer interface (ACI) specifies the commands available to the model, how environment state is returned, and how the interaction history is formatted into each input. The authors draw four principles from manual inspection and a grid search on a development set: actions should be simple, actions should be compact and efficient, environment feedback should be informative but concise, and guardrails mitigate error propagation. The authors assume a fixed language model and change only the interface, without modifying model weights.
sections.heading: The Agent-Computer Interface
sections.headline: The paper defines the agent-computer interface as the layer through which language model agents act on computers, and lists design principles for it.

sections.body: SWE-agent is built on the Linux shell and, at each step, the model generates a thought and a command. The search commands `find_file`, `search_file` and `search_dir` return at most 50 results, and if a search exceeds that number the agent is asked to write a more specific query. The file viewer shows at most 100 lines with line numbers and counts of omitted lines, and the edit command replaces a line range in a single step. An integrated linter discards edits that introduce errors and asks the agent to try again. Context management keeps the last 5 observations in full and collapses earlier ones into single lines. This section describes the design and does not report evaluation results.
sections.heading: SWE-agent: Designing an ACI for Software Engineering
sections.headline: SWE-agent provides search, a file viewer, a linter-guarded edit command and context management for software engineering tasks.

sections.body: Main results use the full SWE-bench test set, while ablations and analyses use the SWE-bench Lite subset of 300 instances. HumanEvalFix tests basic code editing. The models are GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus; the authors report that other models, including Llama 3, performed poorly in the agent setting, and note that Llama 3's context window is 8k. One baseline uses a BM25 retrieval system and asks the model to generate a patch directly. The other, Shell-only, follows the InterCode setup and interacts with a Linux shell. Metrics are % Resolved (pass@1) and average API cost. The per-instance budget is USD 4, after which existing edits are submitted automatically.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Experiments use SWE-bench, its Lite subset and HumanEvalFix, comparing SWE-agent with a retrieval-augmented baseline and a shell-only baseline.

sections.body: Across systems, SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo performs best, with 12.47% on the full test set and 18.00% on the Lite split. Compared with the retrieval-augmented baseline on Lite, it costs 8-13x more and yields a 6.7-fold improved % Resolved rate. The Lite ablations in Table 3 show that without the file editor, performance drops to 10.3%, against 18.00% for the full configuration. A full-file viewer gives 12.7%, and a 30-line viewer gives 14.3%. Iterative search gives 12.0%, versus 15.7% with no search tool. The authors attribute this to agents inspecting every match, which can exhaust cost or context budgets. The ablations are reported on the Lite split only.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo resolves 12.47% of SWE-bench test tasks, and Lite ablations show interface choices change results.

sections.body: This section places the work among code generation benchmarks, which use short problems of about 100 lines with tests that are handwritten or generated by fuzz testing. The authors note that the top method on HumanEval solves 94.4%, so many of these benchmarks are saturating. They argue that software engineering is a more diverse testbed. They use SWE-bench because it combines program repair, bug localization and testing under one task formulation, grounded in real GitHub issues from 12 repositories and evaluated with human-written unit tests. The related work on language model agents covers web navigation, computer control, code generation, offensive security, clinical tasks and theorem proving.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Code benchmarks are largely self-contained, while SWE-bench uses real repository issues, and the authors claim the first language agent study of end-to-end software engineering.

sections.body: The discussion summarizes SWE-agent as a language model plus an ACI that autonomously solves software engineering tasks. The authors state that their design methodology, results and analysis show the value of ACIs tailored to model strengths and weaknesses. They suggest that studying ACIs could improve understanding of language models and agents, in a way comparable to the synergy between human-computer interaction and psychology. They note that humans and language models differ in characteristics, training objectives, specialties and limitations, and that interaction design can serve as systematic behavioral experimentation. These are stated as hopes rather than tested results.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors conclude that interfaces tailored to language model strengths improve results, and suggest studying them may clarify how models differ from humans.

sections.body: The appendix details the file viewer, file editor, and search components, including the edit guardrail and the configuration file, along with prompt templates and trajectory statistics. The ethics discussion says SWE-agent runs in Docker containers, which the authors judge sufficient for code not engineered to exploit container escapes, and it notes risks such as malicious evaluation datasets and offensive use. The reproducibility section lists open source code, documentation, and inference and evaluation artifacts. The stated limitations are that the toolkit is small and that ACI development and case studies were done manually. Future work includes automating ACI design and applying the approach to other domains such as data analysis.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers component designs, sandboxed execution, reproducibility, limitations, and further analyses of trajectories and statistics.
